<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language
<br class="ltx_break">to Leverage Structure and Semantics
<br class="ltx_break">at the LLM Interface</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output.
However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string.
For example, most prompts contain both instructions (“Summarize this paper into a paragraph”) and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “Lemon”), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM.
This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security.
This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases.
We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The natural interface to LLMs, a string of text called a prompt, has been a key component of its success. It enables nontechnical users to leverage the power of LLMs for a wide variety of tasks without having to learn any special language — if a person can communicate via natural language, they can interact with an LLM.
However, the current interface has several shortcomings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A prompt includes the instructions for the particular request. It can also include the data to be used for the request, example results, and constraints on the answers. These constraints can be provided by the LLM deployer (as a system prompt) and/or by the user.
As prompts are specified in natural language, they can be interpreted in many ways, and thus, users often need to experiment with several prompts to have the LLM achieve their desired goal.
This approach has several drawbacks:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">There is no meaningful separation of instructions and data.</span>
In principle, any instruction in the prompt, from any source, can be followed by the LLM, leading to a wide range of attacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawat et al., 2024</a>)</cite> e.g., prompt injection attacks involve inserting instructions via user input, or in content retrieved by an agent that the model should not
follow but does;
Segregation of “data” and “control” is a fundamental principle in computing, but it is not followed in LLMs. Widely-used chat templates (e.g., system/user/assistant role serialization) do not, by themselves, impose execution semantics or reliably enforce instruction-vs-data separation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">There is no referential structure in contexts.</span> Many instructions have implicit “arguments” (e.g. “summarize <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">this document</span>” or “compare <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">these two documents</span>”), but there are only weak ways of “pointing” to these items. LLMs can get lost in long chat contexts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laban et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or lose track of which version of an artifact is the current one.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">There is no explicit control over what should be executed.</span> Any instruction in context can be executed, impacting reliability.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompts are not portable across models.</span>
A prompt that works well for one model may not work well for another model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mizrahi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sclar et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Thus, organizations that optimize their prompts may be leery of changing to a different model. This can result in model dependency, which can result in increased cost and lost opportunity to benefit from the advancements in the broader model provider ecosystem.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLMs are not deterministic.</span>
The same prompt given to the same model can produce different outputs. Although this can be desirable for creative tasks, it is an undesirable behavior, which has deep ramifications for the application development lifecycle that is built on deterministic repeatability.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLMs force a linear data flow.</span>
Output tokens are generated sequentially from the preceding prompt and what was generated so far. Thus, every generated token depends on all tokens that preceded it. Sensitive data contained in the prompt or the generated response can taint everything that is generated after it.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompts are not decomposable into component entries.</span>
A prompt is often a very large string with no logical subcomponents or
abstraction boundaries.
This has the following implications:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.I1.i7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1.i7.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reuse of prompt components is challenging.</span>
As there are no subcomponents of prompts, reuse opportunities are hindered.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompts are not debuggable.</span>
If a prompt is not producing the desirable effect, it is not clear how to modify it to get an improvement.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompts are not maintainable.</span> Prompts are modified to improve results or to react to underlying problem changes. As prompts are a monolith, there is no way to do component versioning (as is done with lines in a code file). Thus, collaboration on prompts is a challenge, similar to collaborating on a binary file stored in <span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">git</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No error checking on prompts.</span>
Prompts are a long string, so any character is valid in the string.
This precludes any kind of consistency checking that we see with programming languages that check for valid syntax or type compatibility.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i7.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No insight/performance analytics about prompt successes and failures.</span>
It can be useful to study successful prompts to learn best practices. As prompts are a monolith, this can be done only at the coarsest granularity, limiting the transfer of insights about prompt performance.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Comparison Between Programming via Prompts with LLMs and Traditional Programming</figcaption>

<tr id="S1.T1.2.7" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S1.T1.2.13.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S1.T1.2.13.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Yes, via tracing, live monitoring, etc.</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes these shortcomings and contrasts them to traditionally programmed systems, which has support for all of these attributes by the specified mechanism.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The main goal of this paper is to propose an LLM-native markup language, called LLMON (LLM Object Notation), to facilitate communicating concepts and structures with LLMs.
This richer metadata information about the underlying text can then be used
during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation,
leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security.
This is analogous to how the types in programming languages can be used for several purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The contributions of this paper are the following:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Identification of shortcomings of the current LLM computation model. These shortcomings can be addressed by an LLM-native markup language.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Enumeration of design requirements and decisions for an LLM-native markup language</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Specification of an enabling technology, a LLM-native markup language, called LLMON, that addresses these design requirements. The language can be expressed in both a human-friendly succinct syntax and as a more LLM-friendly syntax with converters available between both forms.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Description of converters that convert structured representations, such as JSON, into LLMON, allowing existing structured training data to be easily leveraged without modification</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Descriptions for how LLMON information can be leveraged during model training and inference implementation to improve accuracy, safety, and security</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reporting of empirical evidence of the efficacy of the LLMON approach for two use cases, model training and inference implementation, showing significant improvements of
74.2 and 29.3 percentage points, respectively.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Discussions on future research opportunities in the space of LLM-native markup languages</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The rest of this paper is organized as follows.
Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> enumerates some of the desirable properties of an LLM-native markup language.
Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> describes our suggested LLM-native markup language, LLMON, and our approach to making it both human- and LLM-friendly by introducing two equivalent syntaxes.
Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> describes the LLM-friendly syntax called <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.
Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Leveraging LLMON Information ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> describes how information communicated via LLMON can be utilized in model training and inference implementation.
Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Initial Evidence of Value ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> provides an initial evaluation of the value of LLMON.
Section <a href="#S7" title="7 Related Work ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> describes related work.
Section <a href="#S8" title="8 Discussion ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> discusses some of the implications and additional research opportunities enabled by a LLMON approach.
Section <a href="#S9" title="9 Conclusions ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> concludes this work. The appendix provides additional examples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The main goal of the LLM-native markup language is to facilitate the communication of metadata
information to the LLM in a native way. This can be used in a number of ways, such as during training, during prompts, and during inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The next two subsections enumerate important design requirements and considerations for an LLM-native markup language.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Design Requirements</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<dl id="S2.I1" class="ltx_description">
<dt id="S2.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I1.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1. User-defined tag</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The markup language needs to allow the expression of semantic concepts as user-defined tags.
<br class="ltx_break">This will allow the communication of meta information about a text passage, such as whether it is an instruction, data, email, or poem.</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S2.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I1.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2: Named Instances</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The markup language needs to have a mechanism to name text segments with a unique identifier.
<br class="ltx_break">It is useful to be able to refer to other entities within the data, similar to links and anchors in HTML. For example, this can allow instructions to reference certain data.</p>
</div></dd>
</dl>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A general theme in any kind of
LLM-native markup is the importance of the order of markup. Although
order does not matter for regular markup, it is essential to consider
for LLMs as they consume and generate tokens sequentially. This property leads to the next two design requirements.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<dl id="S2.I2" class="ltx_description">
<dt id="S2.I2.ix1" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I2.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3: Explicit Nesting Names</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I2.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Use nesting structures with tags that capture the nesting information explicitly, such as “<span id="S2.I2.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">email.header.from</span>”, rather than a nesting structure with three levels: “<span id="S2.I2.ix1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">email</span>”, “<span id="S2.I2.ix1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">header</span>”, “<span id="S2.I2.ix1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">from</span>”.
<br class="ltx_break">Nesting structures are natural for a hierarchical technology, such as a language parser, but are not as natural to the sequential nature of LLMs. For example, a parser will have no problem with a JSON object that contains thousands of elements because it acts as a pushdown automata <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hopcroft et al., 2006</a>)</cite>, i.e., has a stack to remember what to expect. An LLM works sequentially and does not have this mechanism, so
large nesting structures will require larger context to ascertain information that can be conveyed in a more direct manner.</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S2.I2.ix2" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I2.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4: Prefix</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I2.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The annotation for a text segment should appear before the text segment (prefix) rather than after it (postfix).
<br class="ltx_break">This will enable the LLM to learn the annotation while processing the text. If we want the annotation to impact generation, the annotation must appear before the text that it is annotating. This gives the LLM (and the constrained decoding system) a clear idea of what it should generate next.</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S2.I2.ix3" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I2.ix3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5: Convertibility</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I2.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We should be able to easily convert between existing structured representations, such as JSON, and the markup language in both directions.
<br class="ltx_break">Given the large amount of data that exists in structured formats, it is crucial that an LLM-native markup can represent this data.</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S2.I2.ix4" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I2.ix4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6. No escaping</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I2.ix4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.ix4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">There is no need for “escaping” sequences.
<br class="ltx_break">As the markup language can use special tokens (discussed in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Leveraging LLMON Information ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) to signify meta information, there is no need for “escaping” sequences. For example, JSON uses " to signify the beginning of a string, but if the user wants to have text with this character, it needs to be escaped (“\”). Our markup language should not need this mechanism.</p>
</div></dd>
</dl>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Design Considerations</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the above design requirements that we feel any LLM-native markup language should support, there are also some design choices to be made. We enumerate these below.</p>
<dl id="S2.I3" class="ltx_description">
<dt id="S2.I3.ix1" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I3.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">7. Use of Special Tokens</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I3.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How many special tokens?
<br class="ltx_break">Special tokens are requirements to the tokenizer that certain character strings should be viewed as an atomic token, i.e,. cannot be decomposed or combined with other tokens.
Thus, a LLM-native markup language needs to decide which character sequences will be viewed as special tokens.</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S2.I3.ix2" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S2.I3.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">8. Verbose vs. Parsimonious closing tags</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S2.I3.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some markup languages, like XML, require that every open tag is explicitly closed,
whereas other markup languages
use other syntax to push and pop hierarchical levels, e.g., line breaks in YAML. 
<br class="ltx_break">Likewise, a common pattern in chat templates omits open/close tokens when
they are implied, e.g. <span id="S2.I3.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p><pre id="S2.I3.ix2.p1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">
   &lt;turn&gt;assistant&lt;/role&gt; ... message content ... &lt;/turn&gt;
</pre>
</div>
<div id="S2.I3.ix2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.ix2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given the challenge LLMs have with
nesting that spans a
large number of tokens (see above), it is not clear if explicit or verbose closing tags are useful for learning. Experimentation is needed to understand the best approach.
If a parsimonious approach is adopted, care must be taken to ensure that there is no loss of expressiveness.</p>
</div></dd>
</dl>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Introducing LLMON</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Two key orthogonal properties for understanding the LLMON language are its expressive capability (what concepts can it express) and its syntax (how the capability is written). Both are important design decisions and will likely evolve with empirical experience.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expressivity.</span>
LLMON needs to be able to express the standard data concepts that exist in JSON and most programming languages: basic primitive types (integer, float, boolean, string) and composite types (lists and objects).
However, it also needs to express the first three Design Requirements from Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Design Considerations ‣ 2 Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>: user-defined tags, named instances, and explicit nesting names.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Syntax.</span>
When choosing a syntax one needs to ensure it is as natural as possible for the human that needs to write the syntax, as well as allowing easy mapping to the consumer of the syntax (in our case the LLM). When these goals conflict, one can introduce a human syntax and a machine syntax, where conversion between the two is well-defined.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We take this approach with LLMON. Specifically, we define LLMON to be a human-friendly syntax to express the languages key concepts. We define <span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> to be the more verbose markup language that interacts with an LLM and satifies the design requirements from Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Design Considerations ‣ 2 Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. We provide converters between LLMON and <span id="S3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>, which demonstrates they are equal in expressivity. The rest of this section will describe LLMON expressed in the human-friendly syntax. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> will provide details on the LLM-friendly syntax, <span id="S3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Conceptually, the goal of the LLMON markup language is to provide the capability to highlight various segments (or spans) of text with a special “color” or tag that signifies meta information about that text segment.
For example, in the prompt string in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(A), the green section represents an “instruction” to the LLM and the yellow section represents the “data”.
Enabling these designations provides necessary information for an enforcement mechanism (discussed in Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Leveraging LLMON Information During Model Inference ‣ 5 Leveraging LLMON Information ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>) that prohibits executing anything that is not an “instruction”. This prevents a category of malicious prompt injection attacks. This is analogous to how an operating system treats code segments separately from data segments, which provides a key security protection: the inability to execute data that is masquerading as code.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">(A)</p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">
<span id="S3.F1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="font-size:90%;">

<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#BFFF00;">Suggest a title for the following email:</span></span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF00;">Dear customer support, I am writing about the wifi connection on my recent</span></span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.F1.3.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF00;">flight from JFK to LAX. The quality was poor. I paid $25, and I want a refund.</span></span></span>
</span>
</span>
</span></p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">(B)</p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.F1.5" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="font-size:90%;">

<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">\instruction\</span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">    Suggest a title for the following email:</span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">/instruction/</span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">\data\</span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">    Dear customer support, I am writing about the wifi connection on my recent</span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.6" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">    flight from JFK to LAX. The quality was poor. I paid $25, and I want a refund.</span></span>
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.7" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F1.5.1.1.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">/data/</span></span>
</span>
</span>
</span></p></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>(A) Example Prompt, (B) Prompt in LLMON Notation</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, to express this kind of meta information, we need to identify two quantities: the segment of text and the “color” tag that should be associated with that text. We address these needs by enclosing the text segment inside
phrases that indicate the tag (or “color”) of the segment, which is a popular approach for markup languages. In our case we use the sequence
“<span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">\tagname\</span>”
to indicate the beginning of the segment of type
“<span id="S3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">tagname</span>”
and “<span id="S3.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">/tagname/</span>” to indicate the end of the segment of type
“<span id="S3.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">tagname</span>”.
Using this approach, Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(B) shows how the example in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(A) would be expressed, using the tags:
“<span id="S3.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instruction</span>” and “<span id="S3.p6.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">data</span>”.
This syntax enables annotating text with any tag, such as “<span id="S3.p6.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">int</span>”, “<span id="S3.p6.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">data</span>”, “<span id="S3.p6.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">Spanish</span>”,
or “<span id="S3.p6.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">poem</span>”.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Tags are not limited to be a single identifier. We can
reference tag names, such as “<span id="S3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">attachment:3</span>”,
and explicitly encode hierarchical structures in the tag, such as
“<span id="S3.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">email.paragraph</span>”.
By enabling an explicit naming of tags we allow references to these entities similar to HTML anchors (Design Requirement 2).
By explicitly providing the hierarchical structure in the tag name as opposed to having large nesting structures, we increase the likelihood that an LLM will be able to better learn the structure (Design Requirement 3).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">LLMON assigns special meaning to the “\” and “/” characters. If these characters are desired in the regular text, they must be escaped, using the “\” character.
This use of escaping is present only at the human-friendly LLMON syntax. The <span id="S3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> syntax, discussed in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, does not use escaping, allowing it to satisfy Design Requirement 6. Our LLMON to <span id="S3.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> converter provides the appropriate translation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Examples</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Now that we’ve introduced LLMON we can provide some examples that illustrate its expressive power.
Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows an example using LLMON to describe the execution of one of several instructions. The first three text segments are tagged as instructions using the
“<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr:</span>”
tag where “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr</span>” signifies that the tag of the segment is “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr</span>”. The “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">:</span>” token enables the naming of this particular instruction so that it can be referenced elsewhere.
After these three instructions (“<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr:a</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr:b</span>”,
and “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr:c</span>”) we have an “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec</span>”
section that will indicate which of the instructions should be executed. The “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec:x</span>” tag indicates that it is an exec section with instance name “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">x</span>”.
Inside this section, we have another tag (“<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec:x.instr</span>”) that indicates the instruction instance that should be executed. Here we see the power of having instances names for tag segments because we can reference any of the three instructions to be executed. In this example, it is “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr:b</span>”.
This example also illustrates how we can utilize LLMON’s flattened nesting feature to explicitly describe the nesting in the tag name; i.e., the tag “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec:x.instr</span>” is nested inside the “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec</span>” section. As described in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> this will help model learning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S3.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S3.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="font-size:90%;">

<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="S3.F2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="S3.F2.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.F2.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">\instr:b\  Calculate 12 + 8 /instr:b/</span></span>
<span id="S3.F2.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="S3.F2.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">

</span>
</span>

<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> builds on the previous example by introducing a data section (“<span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">data:1</span>”) that is a parameter to the “<span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec:y.input</span>”
tag, allowing parameters to be passed to the called instruction.
Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows another example that illustrates how LLMON can be used to defend against a prompt injection attack.
This figure is a variant of Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, where we have three instructions and a data section. In this example the data message includes a malicious instruction.
However, even though this <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">data</span> instance is provided to the <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec</span>
as a parameter, the LLM executes only the <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr</span> parameter and the attack fails.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S3.F4.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">

<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Summary of Design Decisions</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Summary of Design Decisions ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes how our approach with LLMON addressed the design requirements mentioned in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
User-defined tags are supported by specifying the tagname before and after the text passage.
Support for naming instances of text is provided by the “<span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">:</span>” token, as in “<span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">instr:a</span>”.
Similarly, the “<span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">.</span>” token enables the specification of nesting via explicit names, such as “<span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">exec:x.instr</span>”.
Our tags use prefix-style notation; the opening of tag occurs before the content it is describing. We have written converters between JSON and LLMON and believe converters for other structured representations are straightforward.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although LLMON does require escaping for expressing characters like “\” and “/”, the language that is provided to the LLM, <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>, does not require escaping.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In terms of design decisions,
we are currently taking a verbose approach to closing tags; i.e., they include the tag name to help with human readability. However, this information is not needed for parsing (in converters) and may not be useful from an LLM-learning capability because this closing tag occurs after the content it describes. We plan to experiment with this approach and a parsimonious approach where the tag name is not present to understand the tradeoffs in learning. If it aids in human understanding, we can keep the closing tag in LLMON, but translate it into a parsimonious version for <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>, which is fed to the tokenizer.
We will describe our design choice for special tokens in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>LLMON Design Decisions</figcaption>
<table id="S3.T2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<th id="S3.T2.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">LLMON Approach</span></th></tr>

<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

<td id="S3.T2.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T2.2.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">supported with “:” special token</span></td></tr>

<td id="S3.T2.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T2.2.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">have converters between JSON and LLMON</span></td></tr>

<td id="S3.T2.2.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T2.2.7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">Machine LLMON<span id="S3.T2.2.7.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> does not use any escaping</span></span></td></tr>

<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>LLMON Grammar</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 LLMON Grammar ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides the grammar for the LLMON markup language. It is constructed to enable a predictive parser to be employed.
The table in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 LLMON Grammar ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>
provides the mapping of grammar terminals to strings.
<span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">user_tag_text</span> is defined via a regular expression below the table. It is the typical programming language rule for identifiers extended to allow <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">‘‘:’’</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">‘‘.’’</span>.
We have created a parser for the language.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="S3.F5.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S3.F5.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.F5.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_th ltx_th_row"></th>
<td id="S3.F5.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.F5.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">LLMON:</span></td>
<td id="S3.F5.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.F5.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">LLMON_ITEM LLMON_LIST</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.F5.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.F5.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_th ltx_th_row"></th>
<td id="S3.F5.2.2.2" class="ltx_td"></td>
<td id="S3.F5.2.2.3" class="ltx_td"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.F5.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.F5.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_th ltx_th_row"></th>
<td id="S3.F5.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.F5.2.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">LLMON_LIST:</span></td>

<p id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.F5.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">user_tag_text<span id="S3.F5.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> is represented by the regular expression:
<br class="ltx_break"><code id="S3.F5.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">[_a-zA-Z][_a-zA-Z0-9.:]*</code>

<br class="ltx_break"></span></span></p></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>LLMON Grammar. terms in UPPER_CASE are nonterminals.
terms in single quotes or lowercase are terminals.
The table provides current values for the nonquoted terminals.
<br class="ltx_break">“<span id="S3.F5.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">user_tag_text</span>” represents a typical identifier extended to include “<span id="S3.F5.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">:</span>” and “<span id="S3.F5.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.</span>” as illustrated in examples in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.
“<span id="S3.F5.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">object</span>”, “<span id="S3.F5.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">item</span>”, and “<span id="S3.F5.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">list</span>” are exactly those strings.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Dealing with Ambiguous Patterns</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In designing LLMON we’ve tried to keep the common patterns easy to express succinctly. One example of this is when expressing strings, there is no need to add quotes, as is done in JSON. This convenience implies additional complexity when there is a desire to express a nonstring.
For example, consider this key/value pair expressed in JSON:
<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p><pre id="S3.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">
    "GPA":3.4
</pre>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The key (like all JSON keys) is a string and the value is a float. Now consider a similar LLMON version
<span id="S3.SS4.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p><pre id="S3.SS4.p1.4" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">
    \item\GPA:3.4/item/
</pre>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.5" class="ltx_p">By default, the 3.4 will be interpreted as a string, which would be correct if the JSON example had quotes around the 3.4.
Thus, to represent the float 3.4 rather than the string 3.4, we need to write it as
<span id="S3.SS4.p1.5.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p><pre id="S3.SS4.p1.6" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">
   \float\3.4/float/
</pre>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.7" class="ltx_p">So, the full example would be
<span id="S3.SS4.p1.7.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p><pre id="S3.SS4.p1.8" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">
    \item\GPA: \float\3.4/float/ /item/
</pre>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.9" class="ltx_p">This is similar to type casting in programming languages and will be particularly relevant when translating LLMON to other structured formats, such as JSON.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The LLMON grammar from Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 LLMON Grammar ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> defines the expressivity of the markup language.
In Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> we described the human-friendly syntax for expressing LLMON concepts.
This section describes <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>, which is the version of the syntax that is more LLM-friendly.
<span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> preserves the structure and semantics of LLMON while expressing them using a small set of special tokens.
This representation is designed to make structural boundaries explicit in the token stream so that both the model and inference-time systems can reliably identify spans such as instructions, data artifacts, and execution bindings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although LLMs appear to take text as input (for training and prompts), this text is actually first transformed into tokens, by a <span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tokenizer</span>.
A token is an integer that can represent segments of the input.
These segments can vary from a single character to multiple words based on an analysis of the patterns in the text.
For example, a phrase like “in the” may occur so often that the tokenizer decides it would ease learning to treat it as a single token, much like humans create acronyms for common phrases, such as “LOL” (Laugh Out Loud) and “TMI” (Too Much Information).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to regular tokens created by the tokenizer, one can also define special tokens, which are character sequences that the tokenizer treats atomically, i.e., it assigns them their own token number and does not decompose or combine them with any adjacent characters.
This is typically done to ensure clarity in what is trying to be expressed with the goal of helping LLM learning.
Examples of special tokens include markers that signify the beginning or ending of a sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Special tokens are a natural way to specify the richer structure of
data to an LLM.
For example, distinguishing which part of a prompt is
an instruction and which is data will need a meta-mechanism that can leverage special tokens.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S4.T3.5.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T3.5.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|open|&gt;tag&lt;|self_close|&gt;</span></td></tr>

<td id="S4.T3.5.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T3.5.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|:|&gt;</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> currently uses special tokens for six syntactic entities shown in the left side of Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
These entities represent the key differences between LLMON and <span id="S4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.
The right side of Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>
shows how these special tokens map LLMON to <span id="S4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> syntax in a straightforward way. The LLMON characters <span id="S4.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">‘‘.’’</span> and <span id="S4.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">‘‘:’’</span> are only mapped to the <span id="S4.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> special tokens when they appear in LLMON tags, reference LLMON tags, or representing key/value pairs. Their use in general text is left as is.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">By designating the strings from the left side of Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> as special tokens, it means that a <span id="S4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> tag such as
“<span id="S4.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">&lt;|open|&gt;email&lt;|close|&gt;</span>”
is guaranteed to have “<span id="S4.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">&lt;|open|&gt;</span>” and “<span id="S4.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">&lt;|close|&gt;</span>” be unique tokens; they will not be combined with any preceding or following text, nor will they be decomposed into multiple tokens.
Similarly, a typename such as “<span id="S4.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">email&lt;|.|&gt;from</span>” will have the “<span id="S4.p6.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">&lt;|.|&gt;</span>” treated as a unique token, which will make it easier for the model to learn its special meaning.
As discussed in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Design Considerations ‣ 2 Desirable Requirements and Considerations for an LLM-Native Markup Language ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, this selection of special tokens is an important design choice that should be evaluated to determine its efficacy. Further evidence may suggest increasing the number of special tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> provides the mapping of nonquoted terminals in the grammar in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 LLMON Grammar ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> to <span id="S4.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.
Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.1 LLMON Workflow ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows how the LLMON example from Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(B) will be written in <span id="S4.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.
Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.1 LLMON Workflow ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows how the example in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> would be expressed in <span id="S4.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Dealing with Ambiguous Patterns ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>, since LLMON uses the characters “\” and “/” to encode special meaning it requires escaping these characters (with “\”) to represent these characters in text.
Since <span id="S4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> instead relies on special tokens to represent this meaning, it does not need to use escaping, satisfying Design Requirement 6.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">

<td id="S4.F6.2.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.8.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|open_end|&gt;item&lt;|close</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.F6.2.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.F6.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_l ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">start_list_tag</span></td>
<td id="S4.F6.2.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.9.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|open|&gt;list&lt;|close|&gt;</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.F6.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.F6.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_l ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.10.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">end_list_tag</span></td>
<td id="S4.F6.2.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.10.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|open_end|&gt;list&lt;|close&gt;</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.F6.2.11" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.F6.2.11.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_l ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.11.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">colon_separator_tag</span></td>
<td id="S4.F6.2.11.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.11.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|:|&gt;</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.F6.2.12" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.F6.2.12.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.12.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">list_separator_tag</span></td>
<td id="S4.F6.2.12.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.F6.2.12.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">&lt;|list-separator|&gt;</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Current values for the nonquoted terminals from Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 LLMON Grammar ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> expressed in <span id="S4.F6.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.
“<span id="S4.F6.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">user_tag_text</span>” is the same as in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 LLMON Grammar ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. It can be any identifier and can include “<span id="S4.F6.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">:</span>” and “<span id="S4.F6.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.</span>” as illustrated in examples in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Examples ‣ 3 Introducing LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.
“<span id="S4.F6.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">object</span>”, “<span id="S4.F6.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">item</span>”, and “<span id="S4.F6.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">list</span>” are exactly those strings.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>LLMON Workflow</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.1 LLMON Workflow ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> illustrates the workflow from human-friendly LLMON markup to the token sequence used during model post-training and inference.
One could author a file (or prompt) in LLMON and have it trivially converted to <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>.
This, as with all input, is passed to the tokenizer, which decomposes the string into tokens that are then used for post-training or inference.
The resulting token sequence is identical to the form consumed by the model during both training and inference, allowing the same structural annotations to influence learning, prompting behavior, and runtime execution mechanisms.
In this sense, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span> acts as a structural interface layer between human-authored prompts and the token-level representation consumed by the LLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Because the delimiters are defined as special tokens, they remain atomic units in the token stream, enabling the model to learn associations between these markers and the surrounding content during training and inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Conceptually, the workflow has three stages.
First, a structured input may be authored in the human-friendly LLMON syntax.
Second, this representation is deterministically converted to <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>, replacing markup delimiters and connectors with the corresponding special tokens.
Finally, the tokenizer maps the resulting string into token identifiers, ensuring that the structural markers appear as stable, identifiable tokens in the model input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This process ensures that structural boundaries (such as the start and end of an instruction span or an execution binding) are visible in the token stream.
Consequently, the model can learn associations between these markers and the surrounding content during training, and inference-time systems can identify the same spans when enforcing structured behaviors such as instruction selection or tool invocation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F7.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S4.F7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="font-size:90%;">

<span id="S4.F7.2.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="S4.F7.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="S4.F7.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F7.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">    Suggest a title for the following email:</span></span>
<span id="S4.F7.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">

<img src="2603.22519v1/LLMON-Flow-v5.png" id="S4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/63;" width="452" height="63" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Workflow from human-authored LLMON markup to the token sequence used during model post-training and inference.
A structured artifact written in the human-friendly LLMON syntax is deterministically converted into <span id="S4.F9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Machine LLMON</span>, where structural delimiters are represented using special tokens (shown in red).
The tokenizer then maps the sequence into token identifiers, preserving structural boundaries in the token stream.
Blue and black tokens represent ordinary text tokens produced by the tokenizer; alternating colors are used only to visually distinguish adjacent tokens and illustrate token boundaries as seen by the tokenizer.
This tokenized representation can be used directly for model post-training and inference procedures.</figcaption>
</figure>

<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>LLMON and JSON</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">JSON is a popular markup language for representing data and is often used to specify the required format for LLM output from a prompt. Thus, it is necessary to show how a JSON structure can be represented in LLMON.
This section describes this information-preserving mapping; i.e., any JSON object converted to LLMON can be converted back to the original JSON.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">JSON has four primitive types (<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">string</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">number</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">boolean</span>, and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">null</span>) and two composite types (<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">object</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">array</span>).</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">object</span> is a comma-separated sequence of key/value pairs, separated by a <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘:’’</span>, where the key is a <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">string</span>, and the value is any of the six types. An object begins with <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘{’’</span> and ends with <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘}’’</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">array</span> is a comma-separated list of values, which can be any of the six types. An <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">array</span> begins with <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘[’’</span> and ends with <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘]’’</span>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.2 LLMON and JSON ‣ 4 Machine LLMON ‣ LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Languageto Leverage Structure and Semanticsat the LLM Interface" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> shows an example JSON object and how it can be expressed in LLMON. The JSON object contains two key/value pairs. The first pair is a simple key/value, where the value is a string (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">"Planned Trips"</span>). The second pair has a value that is a list of strings (<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘New York’’, ‘‘Tokyo’’, ‘‘Egypt’’</span>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F10" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F10.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.F10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JSON</span>
                 
<span id="S4.F10.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLMON
<br class="ltx_break"></span> 

<span id="S4.F10.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="font-size:80%;">

<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">{</span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.1.2" class="ltx_td"></span></span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row"></span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">"Purpose": "Trips"</span></span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row"></span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">"Cities": ["New York", "Tokyo", "Egypt"]</span></span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">}</span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.3.1.4.2" class="ltx_td"></span></span>
</span>
</span>
</span>

 
<span id="S4.F10.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="font-size:80%;">

<span id="S4.F10.2.4.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="S4.F10.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F10.2.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">\object\</span></span>
<span id="S4.F10.2.4.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.F10.2.4.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">      \object.item\Purpose: Trips/object.item/</span></span>
